summary: One of the documents that together define the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). This one describes the abstract model: the printers, jobs, and operations that users and administrators can work with. It is a standards-track document. It was replaced by RFC 8011.

eli5.summary: This describes the idea of a network printer: what a print job is, what a printer can do, and what you can ask it.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what does ipp attribute fidelity do
subtitle: The abstract model behind network printing: Printer and Job objects, the operations on them, and the attributes that describe them.

tldr.problem: Printing over a network needs a common way to find printers, submit jobs, check their progress and manage them, without tying that to one vendor's system or one wire format.
tldr.mechanism: IPP/1.1 defines two abstract objects, Printer and Job, a fixed set of request/response operations on them (Print-Job, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job and others) and the attributes that describe capabilities, jobs and state. The encoding and transport are left to RFC 2910.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2911 obsoleted RFC 2566 (IPP/1.0) but is itself obsoleted by RFC 8011, and several later RFCs updated it, so RFC 8011 is the current definition of the model.

today: RFC 2911 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8011, which is now the definition of the IPP/1.1 model. It was also updated by RFC 3380, RFC 3382, RFC 3995, RFC 3996 and RFC 7472, and it itself obsoleted RFC 2566.

sections.title: A Simplified Model of Printing
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. RFC 2911 is the Model and Semantics document of IPP/1.1. It describes abstract objects, their attributes and their operations, independent of encoding and transport. The encoding and the mapping onto HTTP/1.1 are in RFC 2910.

The model deliberately exposes only the key objects and interfaces needed for printing, even though the real system underneath may be a complex multi-tier client/server arrangement. IPP/1.1 focuses on end-user functions, with a few optional operator operations added. It is part of a set of documents that also includes RFC 2567 (design goals), RFC 2568 (rationale) and RFC 2569 (mapping between LPD and IPP).

Three kinds of people are in the picture. End users submit and track their own jobs. Privileged operators or administrators can cancel, hold, release and restart any user's job and, with optional operations, pause, resume or purge a Printer. Asynchronous notification is out of scope: clients follow progress by polling with the query operations.
sections.eli5: Instead of describing every wire and gear inside a print shop, this document only talks about the front desk: you hand over a job, ask how it is going, or ask to cancel it.

sections.title: Printer and Job Objects
sections.content:
The model has two object types. A Printer object is the server side of the protocol. It stands in for the physical output device together with spooling, scheduling and management of several devices. It may be embedded in a device, or hosted on a server that talks to one or more devices over IPP or another protocol. Because it is an abstraction, the RFC notes it could represent a fax device, an imager or even a CD writer.

A Job object models one print job. The Printer creates it when it accepts a create request. An implementation MUST support at least one document per Job and MAY support several. A document is either a stream of data in a format the Printer supports (typically a page description language) or a reference to such a stream. Documents are not objects in IPP/1.1: they have no identifier or attributes, and all processing instructions are Job attributes that apply equally to every document in the Job.

A Printer contains zero or more Jobs, and a Job belongs to exactly one Printer. Each object is described by attributes that are labelled REQUIRED, RECOMMENDED or OPTIONAL. If an implementation supports an attribute, it MUST support at least one of its possible values.
sections.eli5: A printer is like a bakery counter and each print job is one order ticket. The counter can hold many tickets, but every ticket belongs to exactly one counter.

sections.title: How Objects Are Identified
sections.content:
Every Printer and Job is identified by a URI. A Printer's printer-uri-supported attribute lists one or more URIs, and each may be a different communication channel with its own security, for example an https channel and a plain http channel. Two companion attributes, uri-security-supported (for example tls or none) and uri-authentication-supported (for example digest or none), have the same number of values and say what each URI uses. A client picks exactly one of these URIs as the target of a request.

When the Printer creates a Job it MUST generate both a job-uri and a numeric job-id. The Job URI is built from the Printer's security policy and the channel the client used, so a job submitted over a secure channel gets a secure URI. The job-id is a 32-bit positive integer that is only unique within the Printer that created the Job. Both exist so that clients with different constraints can address a Job either by its URI or by Printer URI plus Job ID. A job-printer-uri attribute on the Job points back to its Printer.

Objects also have names, printer-name and job-name. These need not be unique and only have local meaning. An administrator sets the Printer's name; the client may supply the Job's name, and otherwise the Printer generates one. The RFC recommends registering Printers in a directory service, and Appendix E defines a generic directory schema for that.
sections.eli5: Every printer and every job gets an address, like a house number. A job also gets a short ticket number that only makes sense at the printer that handed it out.

sections.title: Operations on Printers and Jobs
sections.content:
An operation is a request and a response, and IPP operations are synchronous. Every request carries a version-number, an operation-id, a request-id and its required attributes. The client chooses the request-id as an integer from 1 to 2**31 - 1 so it can match responses to outstanding requests. Every response carries a version-number, a status-code and the copied request-id.

In the operation attributes group, attributes-charset MUST come first and attributes-natural-language second. The target attributes follow: printer-uri alone for Printer operations, job-uri alone, or printer-uri followed by job-id for Job operations.

There are three ways to create a Job. Print-Job pushes one document's data inside the request. Print-URI gives a URI and the Printer pulls the data. Create-Job makes an empty Job for several documents, followed by one or more Send-Document or Send-URI requests, the last of which carries last-document set to true. The client SHOULD use Print-Job for single-document jobs. Validate-Job takes the same attributes as Print-Job but creates nothing, so a client can check in advance that an identical Print-Job would be accepted.

The query operations are Get-Printer-Attributes and Get-Job-Attributes, which take a requested-attributes list or group names such as all, and Get-Jobs. Get-Jobs takes limit, which-jobs (completed or not-completed) and my-jobs; without requested-attributes it returns only job-uri and job-id for each job. Cancel-Job is REQUIRED and may be used from creation until the job is completed, canceled or aborted, so some pages may still print. Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer and Purge-Jobs are OPTIONAL operator operations; Pause-Printer must be paired with Resume-Printer.

Validation is split in time. At submission the Printer checks the supplied attributes and the URI scheme. It need not parse the document or check that a referenced URI is reachable, because those checks must be repeated at processing time anyway. Problems found later are reported through the Job's job-state, job-state-reasons and job-state-message, since the success response has already been sent. A Printer short of space may reject a create request with server-error-busy, and a client must be ready to keep submitting until it is accepted.
sections.eli5: You can drop off one paper, or start a folder and add papers to it one at a time and say which one is the last. You can also ask the front desk whether it could take a job before you hand it over.

sections.title: Text, Names and Languages
sections.content:
Some attributes hold text for humans. The text and name syntaxes carry a charset and a natural language. A text value may be up to 1023 octets (the limit called MAX), and a name value up to 255 octets, unless an attribute states a smaller limit such as text(127).

All clients and Printers MUST support the utf-8 charset and MAY support others registered with IANA. If a Printer does not support the charset a client asks for, it rejects the request with client-error-charset-not-supported and answers in utf-8. A Printer that supports several charsets must convert between them as faithfully as it can, though some information may be lost.

Languages work differently. No natural language is required, but a Printer MUST accept any language the client states and MUST NOT reject a request because of its language. If a particular value is in a different language from the request's attributes-natural-language, the client uses the Natural Language Override form (textWithLanguage or nameWithLanguage) for that value. For text the Printer generates itself, such as status messages, it uses the requested language if supported and otherwise its configured one.
sections.eli5: The printer always understands one common alphabet, and it will keep any language you write in, even if it cannot translate its own replies into that language.

sections.title: Unsupported Attributes and Fidelity
sections.content:
Printers differ, so a request may name attributes or values a Printer cannot honor. Every response carries a status-code (the range is 0x0000 to 0x7FFF), such as successful-ok (0x0000), client-error-bad-request (0x0400) or server-error-internal-error (0x0500). When the status is successful-ok-ignored-or-substituted-attributes, successful-ok-conflicting-attributes, client-error-attributes-or-values-not-supported or client-error-conflicting-attributes, the response MUST include an Unsupported Attributes group listing exactly the supplied attributes that the Printer could not honor.

The RFC names three categories. The Printer may not support the attribute at all, in which case it is returned with the out-of-band value unsupported. It may support the attribute but not the supplied value, in which case the value is echoed back. Or the values may each be supported but conflict with one another, such as stapling transparencies, in which case the Printer returns the values it ignored or substituted. The other out-of-band values are unknown (the Printer supports the attribute but cannot tell the value) and no-value (an administrator has not configured one).

The client decides how strict to be with the boolean ipp-attribute-fidelity operation attribute. With true the Printer MUST reject the job if any Job Template attribute is unsupported. With false, or if omitted, the Printer MUST accept the job by ignoring unsupported attributes and substituting supported values. For example, a request for na-letter media might be printed on iso-a4. Every Printer MUST support both modes.

A related question is whether an IPP attribute overrides an instruction embedded in the document data. The REQUIRED pdl-override-supported Printer attribute says attempted or not-attempted. The attempt is not a guarantee, and a Printer that attempts it poorly is still conforming.
sections.eli5: If you ask for something the printer cannot do, it either says no or does its best, depending on whether you said it had to be exactly right. Either way it tells you what it changed.

sections.title: Job Template Attributes
sections.content:
Attributes in the model fall into several groups. Job Template attributes describe how a job should be processed and are optionally supplied by the client in a create request. They include job-priority, job-hold-until, job-sheets, multiple-document-handling, copies, finishings, page-ranges, sides, number-up, orientation-requested, media, printer-resolution and print-quality.

For a Job Template attribute xxx, a Printer that supports it MUST also expose xxx-default (what will be done if the client says nothing and the document has no embedded instruction) and xxx-supported (what it can do). There is one exception: page-ranges has no default attribute. A Printer that does not support xxx treats a client-supplied xxx as unsupported. A client can ask for the job-template group in Get-Printer-Attributes to fetch all of these at once and offer the user only supported choices.

The administrator may change a default between submission and processing, so the default used at processing time may differ from the one at submission. job-priority is the exception: its default is applied at submission time. It runs from 1 (lowest) to 100 (highest), and a Printer that supports it MUST support the full range.

The other attribute groups are Job Description attributes (such as job-uri, job-id, job-state, job-state-reasons and the size and progress counters) and Printer Description attributes (such as printer-name, printer-state, operations-supported, document-format-supported, queued-job-count and printer-is-accepting-jobs). A client should read operations-supported before using an optional operation.
sections.eli5: Job Template attributes are the little checkboxes on a print dialog: how many copies, one side or two, what paper. The printer also publishes which boxes it offers and which ones are ticked by default.

sections.title: Job and Printer States
sections.content:
The REQUIRED job-state attribute has seven standard values: pending (3), pending-held (4), processing (5), processing-stopped (6), canceled (7), aborted (8) and completed (9). An implementation only needs the states that make sense for its device. Normally a job moves from pending to processing and then ends in one of the three terminal states. The job-state-reasons attribute adds detail, and when there is no reason it MUST be none.

A job that is being canceled or aborted stays in its current state for a while, with processing-to-stop-point in its reasons, until activity ceases. A job that finishes can be retained in a restartable condition for an implementation-defined time (the Job Retention phase), then keeps only its history, and is finally removed. After removal, Get-Job-Attributes and Get-Jobs can no longer return it.

The Printer has its own simpler printer-state with three values: idle (3), processing (4) and stopped (5). printer-state-reasons adds detail and each keyword may carry a -report, -warning or -error suffix. If any error reason is present, the Printer MUST be in the stopped state. A paused Printer must still accept new create requests but MUST NOT let any job enter processing.
sections.eli5: A print job moves along like a parcel: waiting, being handled, and finally delivered, canceled or lost. The printer itself is either free, busy or stuck.

sections.title: Versions, Conformance and Extension
sections.content:
Each request and response carries a version-number of the form X.Y. An implementation MUST support version 1.1. If the major version is unsupported the Printer MUST answer server-error-version-not-supported with the closest version it does support, and the client SHOULD retry with a different version. There is no negotiation as such. The encoding of the version number never changes between versions, and protocol elements that are not carried forward are deprecated so they can never be reused with new meaning.

Conformance is split by role. A conforming client MUST support all REQUIRED operations, gracefully handle unexpected groups, attributes, values and status codes in responses, and support client authentication as defined in RFC 2910. A conforming Printer MUST implement the Printer and Job objects and all REQUIRED operations (Print-Job, Validate-Job, Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs, Cancel-Job and Get-Job-Attributes), and MUST ignore unknown operation attributes but reject a request with a supported attribute holding an unsupported value. Print-URI, Create-Job, Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer, Purge-Jobs, Send-Document, Send-URI, Hold-Job, Release-Job and Restart-Job are OPTIONAL.

The IANA Considerations section sets procedures for registering new keyword values, enum values, attributes, attribute syntaxes, operations, attribute groups, status codes and out-of-band values, which are OPTIONAL for conformance. Section 11 gives the formats for registration proposals.

Appendix F lists the differences from IPP/1.0 (RFC 2566), including new optional operations (Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer, Purge-Jobs, Hold-Job, Release-Job, Restart-Job), the uri-authentication-supported attribute and the detailed-status-message and document-access-error attributes.
sections.eli5: Every message says which edition of the rulebook it follows. New features can be added later, as long as older programs can safely ignore what they do not understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is hard to anticipate the security risks in any given IPP environment. A private corporate network may reasonably skip encryption, while a public network may call for it, and printing payroll checks is worth more protection than printing public files. It also notes that denial-of-service attacks on printing resources are not well understood. IPP therefore MUST be able to operate with different security mechanisms and policies, from very strong to none.

Each URI has an authentication mechanism, matched by position to uri-authentication-supported. The mechanism gives the "authenticated user", which becomes the job owner recorded in job-originating-user-name at creation. Job owners can cancel, hold and release their own jobs, but Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer and Purge-Jobs are for operators or administrators, and others get client-error-forbidden, client-error-not-authenticated or client-error-not-authorized as appropriate. How operators are authorized is not specified.

The RFC discusses same-domain printing, printing across security domains (where the Printer must be authenticated and protected from spamming and malicious document content), and print by reference, where no standard method yet lets a remote entity act with the client's credentials. A Printer may restrict what a query returns, even to nothing, without any status difference. Security MUST NOT be weakened when a client sends a lower version number. For sensitive traffic, TLS is the mechanism the text names for message privacy and authentication, with details in RFC 2910.
sections.eli5: The printer needs to know who is asking so it can let you cancel your own job but not someone else's. How strict that is depends on how secret your pages are and who else is on the network.

messages.label: Create-Job
messages.note: No document data. Creates an empty Job.

messages.label: job-uri, job-id, job-state
messages.note: The client now has the Job's URI and ID.

messages.label: Send-Document (last-document false)
messages.note: Adds one document's data (or Send-URI adds a reference).

messages.label: Send-Document (last-document true)
messages.note: Marks the end of the Job.

items.label: pending
items.desc: A candidate to start processing, but not yet processing.

items.label: pending-held
items.desc: Not a candidate for processing until the reasons for the hold go away.

items.label: processing
items.desc: Being analysed, printed or queued for the output device.

items.label: processing-stopped
items.desc: Stopped while processing; resumes when the reasons are gone.

items.label: canceled
items.desc: Canceled by Cancel-Job and the cancellation is complete.

items.label: aborted
items.desc: Aborted by the system, usually during processing.

items.label: completed
items.desc: Finished, with success, warnings or errors.
